sotto_argomento: Set up alert rules, action groups, and alert processing rules in Azure Monitor
domanda:
An administrator provisions a metric alert rule from Cloud Shell by running:

az monitor metrics alert create -n cpu-alert -g rg-prod --scopes <vmResourceId> --condition "avg Percentage CPU > 90"

The --severity parameter is not specified. Which severity is assigned to the new alert rule, and what does that value mean on the Azure Monitor severity scale?
opzione_a: Severity 0, which is the most critical level on the scale.
opzione_b: Severity 2, a mid-range level on a scale that runs from 0 (critical) to 4 (verbose).
opzione_c: Severity 3, because Azure Monitor defaults new rules to an informational level.
opzione_d: Severity 4, the least critical (verbose) level, so that new rules never page on-call staff.
spiegazione: Correct: The az monitor metrics alert create documentation states that --severity is the "Severity of the alert from 0 (critical) to 4 (verbose)" and lists a default value of 2. When --severity is omitted, the rule is created at severity 2, which sits in the middle of the 0-4 scale. Why the others are wrong: (a) Severity 0 is indeed the most critical end of the scale, but it is not the default - it must be set explicitly. (c) Severity 3 is a valid level but is not the CLI default; the documented default value is 2. (d) Severity 4 is the verbose (least critical) end of the scale and is not the default; also, severity does not by itself determine whether notifications are sent - that is controlled by the action groups attached to the rule.

sotto_argomento: Set up alert rules, action groups, and alert processing rules in Azure Monitor
domanda: A metric alert fires on a virtual machine named VM1. At the moment the alert fires, VM1 is in the scope of two enabled alert processing rules: APR1 uses the Apply action groups action to add an action group named AG-OnCall, and APR2 uses the Suppression action. No schedule restricts either rule. What is the result?
opzione_a: AG-OnCall is invoked first, and suppression then stops any further notifications for the same alert.
opzione_b: AG-OnCall is invoked, because the Apply action groups action always takes precedence over Suppression.
opzione_c: No action groups are invoked for the fired alert, but the alert instance is still visible on the Alerts page in the Azure portal.
opzione_d: The alert rule is prevented from evaluating, so no alert instance is created at all.
spiegazione: Correct: The alert processing rules documentation states that "The suppression action has a higher priority over the Apply action groups action. If a single fired alert is affected by different alert processing rules of both types, the action groups of that alert will be suppressed." Suppression removes all action groups from the affected fired alert, so AG-OnCall is not called. The same documentation confirms suppressed alerts "will still be visible when you list your alerts in the portal, Azure Resource Graph, API, or PowerShell." Why the others are wrong: (a) Suppression removes the action groups entirely; AG-OnCall is never invoked, not invoked-then-stopped. (b) This inverts the documented precedence - Suppression wins over Apply action groups. (d) Alert processing rules act on alerts as they are being fired; they modify alert behavior but do not stop the alert rule from evaluating or the alert instance from being created. Disabling the alert rule itself would be needed to prevent the alert.

sotto_argomento: Set up alert rules, action groups, and alert processing rules in Azure Monitor
domanda: Fabrikam runs 40 Azure virtual machines in a single subscription: 25 in the East US region and 15 in the West Europe region. The operations team wants to be alerted whenever the Percentage CPU platform metric on any of these VMs exceeds 85%, and wants to create as few metric alert rules as possible. What is the minimum number of metric alert rules required?
spiegazione: Correct: A single metric alert rule can monitor multiple resources of the same type only when those resources "exist in the same Azure region", and virtual machines (Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines) are on the list of resource types supported for multi-resource metric alerts. Because the VMs span two regions, you need one multi-resource rule for East US and one for West Europe: two rules total. Individual notifications are still sent for each monitored resource. Why the others are wrong: (a) One rule cannot span East US and West Europe - the scope of a multi-resource metric alert rule is constrained to a single Azure region. (c) 25 would imply one rule per VM in East US only, ignoring that multi-resource rules exist and ignoring the West Europe VMs. (d) 40 (one rule per VM) works but is not the minimum, and it consumes 40 of the 5,000 metric alert rules allowed per subscription unnecessarily. Note that Percentage CPU is a platform (host) metric, so the multi-resource restriction on VM guest metrics does not apply here.

sotto_argomento: Set up alert rules, action groups, and alert processing rules in Azure Monitor
domanda: While building an action group in Azure Monitor, an engineer must distinguish between entries configured on the Notifications tab and entries configured on the Actions tab. Which of the following are action types (automated actions) rather than notification types? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
spiegazione: Correct: The action groups documentation splits action group members into two tables. The Action types table lists exactly these entries: Automation Runbook, Event hubs, Functions, ITSM, Logic apps, Secure webhook, and Webhook. Secure webhook (a), Automation Runbook (c), and Event hubs (e) all appear in that table, so they are automated actions configured on the Actions tab. Why the others are wrong: (b) SMS is listed in the Notification types table, not the Action types table - it is a notification sent to a phone number and supports bi-directional replies such as DISABLE, ENABLE, STOP, and START. (d) Azure app push notifications is also a notification type; it sends notifications to the Azure mobile app based on the Azure account email address. The full notification types list is: Email Azure Resource Manager role, Email, SMS, Azure app push notifications, and Voice.
tags: azure monitor,action groups,action types,notification types,webhook,runbook,event hubs

sotto_argomento: Set up alert rules, action groups, and alert processing rules in Azure Monitor
domanda: Litware defines several action groups that notify different escalation tiers. While configuring the Actions tab of a single metric alert rule, an engineer tries to attach action groups for the database team, the network team, the platform team, the security team, the on-call rotation, and an ITSM bridge. What is the maximum number of action groups that can be added to a single alert rule?
opzione_d: There is no limit on action groups per alert rule.
spiegazione: Correct: The action groups documentation states under Reusability and execution: "You can add up to five action groups to a single alert rule." The engineer's six action groups exceed that limit, so the actions would need to be consolidated into fewer action groups. Why the others are wrong: (a) An alert rule can have more than one action group - and in fact action groups are optional on an alert rule entirely. (c) 10 is the documented per-action-group limit for several individual action types (for example, 10 SMS actions, 10 webhook actions, 10 Logic app actions in an action group), not the number of action groups per alert rule. (d) There is no limit on the number of action groups you can create in a subscription, but there is a hard limit of five action groups attached to one alert rule. Note also that action groups are executed concurrently, in no specific order, and one action group can be reused by many alert rules.

sotto_argomento: Set up alert rules, action groups, and alert processing rules in Azure Monitor
domanda:
Contoso needs a metric alert rule on a production virtual machine with the following requirements:

- The rule must evaluate the average of the Percentage CPU metric over five-minute periods of data.
- The rule must perform that evaluation as often as Azure Monitor allows for metric alerts.
- Fired alerts must carry the most critical severity on the Azure Monitor 0-4 scale.
- While the high-CPU condition persists, the rule must not keep firing; it must fire once and send a resolved notification when the condition clears.

Select the appropriate value for each setting on the alert rule.
opzione_a: Lookback period (aggregation granularity): [1 minute | 5 minutes | 15 minutes]
opzione_b: Check every (evaluation frequency): [1 minute | 5 minutes | 30 minutes]
spiegazione: Correct: Lookback period = 5 minutes. In the When to evaluate section, "Lookback period" selects "how far back to look each time the data is checked" - this is the aggregation window over which the Average aggregation type is applied, so five-minute periods of data means a 5-minute lookback. (The Azure CLI equivalent is --window-size, described as "Time over which to aggregate metrics", default 5m.) Check every = 1 minute. "Check every" selects how often the alert rule checks whether the condition is met; 1 minute is the finest evaluation frequency for metric alerts and is the documented CLI default (--evaluation-frequency, default 1m). Note that evaluation frequency and lookback period are independent: every 1 minute, look back 5 minutes. Severity = Sev0. Severity runs "from 0 (critical) to 4 (verbose)", so the most critical level is Sev0. Sev2 is the mid-range default and Sev4 is the least critical (verbose) end. Automatically resolve alerts = Enabled. This checkbox makes the alert stateful: a stateful alert fires when the conditions are met and "will not fire again or trigger any more actions until the conditions are resolved", and a resolved notification is sent when the condition clears (for metric alerts, when the condition is not met for three consecutive checks). If the checkbox is cleared, metric alerts are stateless and fire each time the condition is met, which is exactly what the requirement forbids.
tags: azure monitor,metric alert,evaluation frequency,lookback period,aggregation granularity,severity,stateful

sotto_argomento: Set up alert rules, action groups, and alert processing rules in Azure Monitor
domanda: The on-call team at Woodgrove Bank reports that a single ongoing high-CPU incident on one virtual machine produced dozens of email notifications over the course of an hour, all referencing the same condition. Reviewing the metric alert rule, you find that the condition, threshold, and action group are all correct, the rule is set to Check every 1 minute with a 5-minute lookback period, and in Advanced options the Automatically resolve alerts checkbox is cleared. What is happening, and what is the appropriate remediation?
opzione_a: The rule is stateless, so it fires every time the condition is met even though it already fired. Select Automatically resolve alerts to make the rule stateful so it will not fire again until the condition resolves.
opzione_b: The evaluation frequency is too aggressive. Increase the lookback period to 24 hours so that the metric is aggregated over a longer window and the rule can only fire once per day.
opzione_c: The action group is being invoked repeatedly by Azure Monitor retries. Create an alert processing rule with a recurring suppression schedule that is active 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.
opzione_d: The severity is set too high. Lower the severity from Sev0 to Sev4 so that Azure Monitor throttles notifications for the rule.
spiegazione: Correct: The Automatically resolve alerts checkbox controls whether a metric alert is stateful or stateless. The documentation says: "If you don't select this checkbox, metric alerts are stateless. Stateless alerts fire each time the condition is met, even if alert already fired." It further states that for a stateless rule with a frequency of less than 5 minutes, "While the condition continues to be met, a notification is sent sometime between one and six minutes" - which precisely matches dozens of notifications in an hour at a 1-minute frequency. Selecting the checkbox makes the alert stateful, so it fires once and does not trigger actions again until the condition resolves (for metric alerts, after the condition is not met for three consecutive checks), at which point a resolved notification is sent. Why the others are wrong: (b) The lookback period is the aggregation window, not a firing cap. Stretching it to 24 hours would badly distort the average CPU signal and delay detection, and a stateless rule would still re-fire on each evaluation. (c) The repeats are caused by stateless re-firing, not by webhook/action retries. A 24x7 suppression alert processing rule would remove all action groups from these alerts, meaning the team would receive no notification at all for genuine incidents. (d) Severity is metadata used for classification, filtering, and routing; it does not throttle notifications. Rate limiting is applied per subscription, per alert rule, and per notification target regardless of severity.
tags: azure monitor,metric alert,stateful,stateless,automatically resolve alerts,troubleshooting,notification noise

sotto_argomento: Set up alert rules, action groups, and alert processing rules in Azure Monitor
domanda: You are configuring the Scope tab of an alert processing rule and want to narrow the rule so that it affects only a specific subset of the fired alerts in its scope. Which of the following are available filters on an alert processing rule? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
spiegazione: Correct: The alert processing rules documentation lists the available filters as: Alert context (payload), Alert rule ID, Alert rule name, Description, Monitor condition, Monitor service, Resource, Resource group, Resource type, and Severity. Severity (a) filters on the selected severities. Monitor condition (b) filters on either Fired or Resolved. Resource type (d) filters on resource types such as virtual machines, and supports Contains to match a resource type and all its child resources. Why the others are wrong: (c) Aggregation type (Sum, Count, Average, Min, Max) is a property of a metric alert rule's condition, configured in the alert rule wizard - it is not an alert processing rule filter. (e) The threshold value of the signal is likewise part of the alert rule's condition definition, not an alert processing rule filter. Remember that multiple filters on one rule are combined with a logical AND, while multiple values within a single filter (up to five) are combined with a logical OR.
tags: azure monitor,alert processing rules,filters,severity,monitor condition,resource type,scope

sotto_argomento: Set up alert rules, action groups, and alert processing rules in Azure Monitor
domanda: An operations engineer working in Azure public cloud creates a Service Health alert rule so that the team is notified by email and SMS about Azure outages and planned maintenance affecting the subscription. When creating the action group, which region must be selected for the action group to function correctly with Service Health alerts?
opzione_b: The same region as the resources that Service Health reports on
opzione_c: Sweden Central, because Service Health notifications are processed only in Europe
opzione_d: Regional, so that the action group is zone-redundant within the subscription's home region
spiegazione: Correct: The action groups documentation states explicitly: "Service Health Alerts are only supported in public clouds within the global region. For Action groups to properly function in response to a Service Health Alert, the region of the action group must be set to Global." With the Global option, the action group is persisted in at least two regions for regional resiliency, and voice, SMS, and email actions performed as the result of service health alerts are resilient to Azure live-site incidents - which is exactly what you want when the alert is telling you Azure itself is having a problem. Why the others are wrong: (b) The action group region is a processing/storage region choice for the action group resource; it is not tied to the regions Service Health reports on, and any non-Global choice breaks Service Health alerts. (c) Sweden Central is one of the valid regions in the Regional processing list, but Regional processing is not supported for Service Health alerts, and there is no rule confining Service Health processing to Europe. (d) Regional processing does give a zone-redundant action group stored within a chosen geographic boundary, and it is the right choice when you must keep processing inside a specific geography - but it is explicitly not supported for Service Health alerts.
tags: azure monitor,action groups,service health,global region,regional processing,activity log alert

sotto_argomento: Set up alert rules, action groups, and alert processing rules in Azure Monitor
domanda:
Adventure Works patches its infrastructure during a weekly maintenance window every Saturday from 00:00 to 06:00. An administrator creates an alert processing rule named APR-Maintenance in a resource group in subscription Sub1. The rule's scope is set to the entire subscription Sub1, the rule action is set to Suppression, and the Scheduling tab is configured with a Recurring weekly schedule covering Saturday 00:00 to 06:00.

Evaluate each of the following statements about APR-Maintenance and determine whether it is true (Yes) or false (No):

1. Resources hosted in a different subscription, Sub2, can be covered by APR-Maintenance if the administrator adds them to the rule's scope.
2. During the Saturday maintenance window, alerts that fire on resources in Sub1 are still visible on the Alerts page in the Azure portal, even though no action groups are invoked for them.
3. During the Saturday maintenance window, APR-Maintenance also suppresses notifications for any Azure Service Health alerts that fire in Sub1.
opzione_a: Resources hosted in a different subscription, Sub2, can be covered by APR-Maintenance if the administrator adds them to the rule's scope.
opzione_b: During the Saturday maintenance window, alerts that fire on resources in Sub1 are still visible on the Alerts page in the Azure portal, even though no action groups are invoked for them.
opzione_c: During the Saturday maintenance window, APR-Maintenance also suppresses notifications for any Azure Service Health alerts that fire in Sub1.
spiegazione:
Statement 1 = No. The documentation states that an alert processing rule applies "to alerts that fired on resources within that scope" and that the scope must be "within the same subscription as the alert processing rule": "You can't create an alert processing rule on a resource from a different subscription." Because APR-Maintenance lives in Sub1, resources in Sub2 cannot be added to its scope; a separate alert processing rule would have to be created in Sub2.

Statement 2 = Yes. The Suppression action "removes all the action groups from the affected fired alerts. So, the fired alerts won't invoke any of their action groups, not even at the end of the maintenance window. Those fired alerts will still be visible when you list your alerts in the portal, Azure Resource Graph, API, or PowerShell." Suppression stops notifications, not alert generation - which is exactly why suppression is preferred over disabling alert rules during maintenance.

Statement 3 = No. The alert processing rules documentation contains an explicit note: "Alert processing rules don't affect Azure Service Health alerts." Service Health alerts will continue to invoke their action groups during the maintenance window regardless of APR-Maintenance.
tags: azure monitor,alert processing rules,suppression,maintenance window,scheduling,service health,scope

sotto_argomento: Set up alert rules, action groups, and alert processing rules in Azure Monitor
domanda: A cloud administrator is documenting how action groups behave before rolling out a standardized alerting design across the organization. Which of the following statements about Azure Monitor action groups are true? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: An action group can contain a maximum of 10 SMS actions.
opzione_b: An action group can contain up to 1,000 email actions.
opzione_c: The same action group can be referenced by multiple alert rules.
opzione_d: An action group can be associated with only one alert rule at a time.
opzione_e: The actions inside an action group are executed sequentially, in the order in which they are listed on the Actions tab.
spiegazione: Correct: (a) The Azure Monitor service limits table for action groups lists "10 SMS actions in an action group" (with a production rate limit of no more than one SMS message every five minutes). (b) The same table lists "1,000 email actions in an action group", along with a rate limit of no more than 100 emails every hour for each email address per region. Note that 10 is the per-action-group cap for most other action types - Azure app push, Event Hubs, ITSM, Logic app, Runbook, Secure webhook, Voice, Webhook, and Email Azure Resource Manager role - which makes Email the notable exception at 1,000. (c) The documentation states "Multiple alert rules can use the same action group" and gives the example of creating a single action group to notify User1, User2, and User3 by email and applying it to two different alert rules. Why the others are wrong: (d) This directly contradicts the documented reusability of action groups; reuse is in fact the recommended pattern, since action groups "are defined by the unique set of actions and the users to be notified." (e) The documentation states "Action groups are executed concurrently, in no specific order" - you cannot rely on the listed order to sequence actions. If you need ordered or conditional logic, use a Logic apps action to orchestrate it.

sotto_argomento: Set up alert rules, action groups, and alert processing rules in Azure Monitor
domanda:
Northwind collects Windows security events from 60 virtual machines into a Log Analytics workspace named LAW1. You must create a log search alert rule scoped to LAW1 that meets these requirements:

- The rule must count the number of matching rows returned by a KQL query against the Event table (it must not perform a calculation on a numeric column).
- Matching rows must be aggregated into 15-minute windows.
- The query must run every 5 minutes.
- A separate alert must be fired for each virtual machine that meets the condition, and each alert must target the virtual machine itself rather than LAW1.

Select the appropriate value for each setting in the alert rule wizard.
opzione_a: Measure: [Table rows | Calculation of a numeric column | Custom metric]
opzione_c: Frequency of evaluation: [1 minute | 5 minutes | 15 minutes]
opzione_d: Split by dimensions on column: [_ResourceId | TimeGenerated | Severity]
spiegazione: Correct: Measure = Table rows. The documentation states that log search alerts can measure two things: "Table rows: You can use the number of returned rows to work with events such as Windows event logs, Syslog, and application exceptions" and "Calculation of a numeric column" for numeric calculations such as CPU percentage. Counting matching Event rows is the Table rows measure. Custom metric is not a log search alert Measure option at all. Aggregation granularity = 15 minutes. Aggregation granularity is documented as the Window size: "The interval for aggregating multiple records to one numeric value." This is a distinct setting from how often the rule runs. Frequency of evaluation = 5 minutes. "Frequency of evaluation: How often the query is run. You can set it anywhere from one minute to one day (24 hours)." The requirement says every 5 minutes; note the documented note that "The frequency is not a specific time that the alert runs every day. It's how often the alert rule runs", and that granularity and frequency are configured independently. Split by dimensions on _ResourceId. The documentation explains that when the alert rule scope is a workspace, alerts fire on the workspace by default; to fire a separate alert per affected Azure resource you split by dimensions on the Azure Resource ID column - "Splitting on the Azure resource ID column makes the specified resource into the alert target." TimeGenerated is a datetime column used for time filtering, not a meaningful resource dimension, and Severity would group alerts by event severity rather than by virtual machine.
tags: azure monitor,log search alert,measure,table rows,aggregation granularity,frequency of evaluation,split by dimensions,log analytics

sotto_argomento: Set up alert rules, action groups, and alert processing rules in Azure Monitor
domanda:
Case study: Tailwind Traders runs its production estate in a single Azure subscription named Sub1. The platform team has grown its alerting footprint to roughly 180 metric alert rules and 40 log search alert rules, all created by different application teams. A single action group named AG-Platform contains the operations distribution list and a Logic apps action that opens a ticket. Two problems have emerged. First, application teams routinely forget to attach AG-Platform when they create new alert rules, so incidents go unticketed until someone notices. Second, Tailwind Traders also relies on built-in Azure Backup alerts for backup failures and soft-delete changes; these alerts are generated automatically and the alert rule experience does not let the team specify an action group for them, so backup incidents never reach AG-Platform at all.

The team wants a single, low-maintenance configuration that routes every fired alert in Sub1 - including alerts that no alert rule generated - to AG-Platform, without editing the 220 existing alert rules. What should the team implement?
opzione_a: Create an alert processing rule scoped to Sub1 that uses the Apply action groups action to add AG-Platform.
opzione_b: Create an Azure Policy assignment with a deployIfNotExists effect that appends AG-Platform to every Microsoft.Insights/metricAlerts and Microsoft.Insights/scheduledQueryRules resource in Sub1.
opzione_c: Enable the recommended out-of-the-box alert rules on every resource in Sub1 and attach AG-Platform to each of them.
opzione_d: Create an alert processing rule scoped to Sub1 that uses the Suppression action, and add AG-Platform to the alert processing rule.
spiegazione: Correct: This is the canonical use case for the Apply action groups action on an alert processing rule. The documentation's Management at scale section explains that instead of manually ensuring each alert rule has the right action groups as the rule count grows, "Alert processing rules allow you to specify that logic in a single rule, instead of having to set it consistently in all your alert rules." Crucially, the Add action groups to all alert types section addresses the second problem directly: "not all Azure alert sources let you specify action groups. Some examples of such alerts include Azure Backup alerts, VM Insights guest health alerts, Azure Stack Edge, and Azure Stack Hub. For those alert types, you can use alert processing rules to add action groups." A rule scoped to the whole subscription Sub1 covers all fired alerts on resources in that subscription, existing and future, without touching the 220 rules. Why the others are wrong: (b) Azure Policy can create alert rules at scale (the Azure Monitor baseline alerts pattern uses it), but the documentation warns this brings "the increased overhead of maintaining a large alert rule set", it would still require modifying the existing rules, and - decisively - it cannot help with built-in Azure Backup alerts, which are not generated by any alert rule resource for a policy to target. (c) Recommended out-of-the-box alert rules are only offered for virtual machines, AKS resources, and Log Analytics workspaces. They create additional new alert rules rather than routing existing ones, do nothing for Azure Backup alerts, and would add to the maintenance burden rather than reduce it. (d) This inverts the required action. Suppression "removes all the action groups from the affected fired alerts", so it would stop notifications entirely rather than deliver them. Suppression is used for planned maintenance windows or out-of-hours quiet periods; Apply action groups is used to add notification routing.
tags: azure monitor,alert processing rules,apply action groups,management at scale,azure backup alerts,action groups
